headline: COPPER HEADS FOR 5TH STRAIGHT WEEKLY LOSS — LME AT $13,500 AS AI SELLOFF HAMMERS ELECTRIFICATION METALS
snippet: LME three-month copper settled at $13,519 per metric ton on Friday November 14 — its worst week since March — as the same AI-related equity selloff that triggered October's tech correction rippled into industrial metals, repricing the demand assumptions underpinning copper's electrification premium. The fifth consecutive weekly loss brings copper down roughly 7% over 30 days. The bearish headline masks a sharply divergent physical picture: Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouse stocks fell to 27,642 tonnes this week, the lowest since December 2023, and the Yangshan copper import premium hit a record $285 per tonne — signalling that Chinese end-users are actively paying up for physical supply even as futures traders exit. For junior copper equity investors, the split between financial-market copper (weak) and physical-market copper (tight) is the key data point: historically this divergence resolves by LME recovering toward physical reality, not the other way around.

headline: GENESIS-VAULT GOLD MERGER 99.74% APPROVED — WA SUPREME COURT MONDAY; DEAL TARGETS NOVEMBER 26 SETTLEMENT
snippet: Vault Minerals shareholders voted 99.74% in favour of the scheme of arrangement with Genesis Minerals at the Scheme Meeting on November 11 — the strongest possible endorsement for the merger that will create one of Western Australia's largest mid-tier gold producers. The final approval gate is a Supreme Court of Western Australia hearing set for Monday November 16; with shareholder support at this level, procedural approval is widely expected. The deal is then set to become effective November 17 and settle November 26. The combined entity will consolidate significant Yandal greenstone belt gold production, with Genesis retaining operational control. For Canadian and Australian junior mining investors tracking consolidation trends, the near-unanimous approval level illustrates how the correction in gold equities is accelerating merger acceptance among smaller producers who see balance sheet pooling as the best defence against a prolonged $3,800–$3,900 gold environment.

headline: EAGLE NUCLEAR BIDS 92% PREMIUM FOR NOBLE PLAINS URANIUM — POWDER RIVER BASIN WYOMING IN ALL-STOCK LOI
snippet: Eagle Nuclear Energy (NASDAQ: NUCL) signed a binding letter of intent on November 4 to acquire all of Noble Plains Uranium (TSX-V: NOBL) in an all-stock transaction at a 92% premium to Noble Plains' October 29 closing price. Noble Plains' primary asset is an option to acquire an 80% interest in the Duck Creek project in Wyoming's Powder River Basin — a 5.32 million pound U3O8 indicated resource plus 1.04 million pounds inferred — plus the earlier-stage Shirley Central project in the Shirley Basin. Noble Plains shareholders would receive 0.0167 Eagle shares per share and hold approximately 4.78% of the combined entity. A 60-day due-diligence and exclusivity period runs to early January; a definitive agreement is targeted before that deadline. The deal illustrates a consolidation pattern emerging among small uranium juniors: US-listed operators are using their stronger equity currencies to roll up TSX-V names with Wyoming basin assets, adding geological inventory without diluting their own shareholders at scale.

headline: PENTAGON DIRECTS $2 BILLION TO NATIONAL DEFENSE STOCKPILE — RARE EARTHS, TUNGSTEN, TITANIUM, ANTIMONY TARGETED
snippet: The Defense Logistics Agency has committed $2 billion in fiscal year 2026 to acquire strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile — funding sourced from the 2025 reconciliation law with a spending window through fiscal 2029. Target materials include rare earths, tungsten, titanium, antimony, high-purity aluminium and vanadium pentoxide. The DLA has also issued a separate $300 million solicitation for battery-grade lithium carbonate. For junior mining investors, the stockpile program creates a category of off-take demand that is structurally independent of EV market cycles and Chinese processor competition: government buyers procure on supply-security logic, not spot price economics. Projects in friendly jurisdictions — Canada, Australia, the US itself — with resources in the targeted commodities have a non-dilutive demand pathway that is growing materially in size. The DLA has previously awarded a contract with a $2 billion ceiling to tungsten specialist Elmet Technologies, though a ceiling is purchasing authority, not guaranteed revenue.

headline: AMERICAN RARE EARTHS BEGINS US NdPr METAL PRODUCTION TESTING — HALLECK CREEK WY MOVES TOWARD DOMESTIC MAGNET CHAIN
snippet: American Rare Earths (ASX: ARR) has started small-scale neodymium-praseodymium oxide and metal production testing at the Novex metallurgy research facility in Washington State — the first step toward validating a fully domestic US rare earth metal supply chain anchored at its Halleck Creek project in Wyoming. The testwork is designed to demonstrate that Halleck Creek ore can be processed into NdPr oxide and then converted into NdPr metal suitable for rare earth permanent magnet (REPM) production, the core input for EV motors and defence actuators. For junior rare earth investors, the Halleck Creek story turns on three variables: processing chemistry proof, capital cost for a commercial plant, and long-term off-take. The Novex testwork addresses the first. Halleck Creek is one of the largest undeveloped rare earth deposits in the United States and sits in a jurisdiction without Chinese processing dependency — the strategic rationale that now attracts OEM and government buyer interest regardless of spot rare earth prices.

headline: RARE EARTHS AMERICAS DOUBLES HOMER PROJECT FOOTPRINT — 60%+ MINERALIZED ZONE EXPANSION IN BRAZIL
snippet: Rare Earths Americas reported that its latest drilling and mapping results at the Homer rare earth project in Brazil have expanded the known mineralized footprint by more than 60%, more than doubling the size of the zone identified in earlier work. The Homer project is a carbonatite-hosted system in a jurisdiction with an established regulatory framework for critical minerals — a structure that attracts institutional attention because carbonatites tend to host high-grade, amenable rare earth mineralisation. For junior investors, a 60%-plus footprint expansion at this stage of exploration is a material discovery-risk reduction event: it confirms the system is not a narrow vein but a broad mineralized body with scale potential. Assay results and an updated resource estimate timeline were not disclosed in the initial announcement.

headline: CANSTAR DRILLS RECORD 15.6m @ 2.4% CuEq AT MARY MARCH — VMS FEEDER ZONE CONFIRMED IN NEWFOUNDLAND BUCHANS DISTRICT
snippet: Canstar Resources (TSX-V: ROX) has intersected the widest massive sulphide interval in the Mary March project's history — 15.6 metres grading 2.4% copper-equivalent in drill hole MM-26-42 — confirming a VMS feeder zone in Newfoundland's Buchans mining district, the same camp that hosted one of North America's highest-grade historic VMS mines. Three of the four holes in the current program cut massive sulphide. The fall program is funded in part by a C$4.0 million total advance from earn-in partner VMS Mining Corporation (VMSC), which increased its Phase 1 investment to C$2.0 million and has since added a further C$2.0 million to advance the fall drilling. For junior copper investors monitoring emerging VMS systems, the Buchans district pedigree and the feeder-zone confirmation geometry are the two most significant technical signals: feeder zones in Buchans-type settings tend to be the conduit to stacked massive sulphide lenses at depth, which is where the high-grade economic core of a VMS system typically lies.

headline: UZBEKISTAN TARGETS URANIUM OUTPUT DOUBLING TO 15,000 TONNES BY 2030 — NAVOIYURAN EXPANDS AS WEST DIVERSIFIES FROM KAZATOMPROM
snippet: Uzbekistan's state uranium producer Navoiyuran has announced plans to roughly double output from approximately 7,500 tonnes per year currently to 15,000 tonnes by 2030 — positioning the Central Asian country as a significant alternative supply source as Western utilities accelerate diversification away from Kazatomprom following the geopolitical disruptions of 2022–2024. At current uranium spot prices near $91/lb, a 15,000 tonne output target represents roughly $3 billion in annual revenue at capacity — a material expansion of non-Russian, non-Chinese primary uranium supply. For the junior uranium sector, the Uzbekistan expansion is a macro-level supply signal worth monitoring: it is new primary uranium supply, but it arrives into a market where long-term utility contracting has re-established a floor, and where most Western demand sits with producers operating in Canada, Australia, Namibia and Kazakhstan. The more pertinent read for TSX-V uranium names is whether Navoiyuran's growth delays or accelerates long-term contract renewals by US and European utilities — the pipeline that underpins most junior project economics.

headline: CRITICAL METALS CLOSES TANBREEZ DEAL — GREENLAND'S MULTI-COMMODITY RARE EARTH DEPOSIT NOW 100% OWNED
snippet: Critical Metals (NASDAQ: CRML) completed its acquisition of European Lithium Limited on November 5, gaining full ownership of the Tanbreez rare earth project in southern Greenland — a large, undeveloped multi-commodity deposit hosting rare earths, zirconium, niobium and tantalum in a syenite host. The deal closes a consolidation that Critical Metals has been building toward since listing on NASDAQ, and gives it a rare earth project with strategic positioning: Greenland is an autonomous territory with its own minerals policy, sits outside EU critical minerals framework constraints, and has attracted recent attention from both US and European industrial buyers seeking non-Chinese rare earth supply. The project has not yet reached bankable feasibility, but full ownership gives Critical Metals the management flexibility to advance permitting, complete metallurgical testwork, and engage off-take discussions without a joint-venture partner. For junior rare earth investors, Tanbreez occupies a speculative tier — large resource, high permitting complexity, long timeline — but the NASDAQ listing gives it access to US institutional capital that TSX-V-only names typically cannot reach.

headline: WHY JUNIOR GOLD STOCKS FALL 3X HARDER THAN GOLD — THE OPERATING LEVERAGE MATH THAT PUNISHES TSXV HOLDERS IN A CORRECTION
snippet: With the GDXJ junior gold miners ETF down 20–30% while spot gold has fallen roughly 15% from its 2026 peak, Discovery Alert's November 2026 analysis maps the structural reason self-directed investors consistently underestimate draw-down risk in gold equity: operating leverage. At $4,500 gold with $1,900 AISC, a junior produces margin of $2,600/oz — if gold falls 15% to $3,825, that margin compresses to $1,925, a 26% reduction. Applied to earnings, the equity typically re-rates even further. The same math that generates 2–4x gold returns in a bull market generates 2–4x gold losses in a correction. The analysis argues the November pullback is consistent with prior corrective phases in gold equity bull markets — Q4 2016, Q4 2020 — where GDXJ fell 30–40% before resuming the primary uptrend. The key variable for recovery timing: whether the FOMC minutes (Wednesday) show any internal dissent on the December hike path, which would shift the rate-cut repricing timeline that institutional investors are waiting on before rebuilding positions.

headline: TWO ELECTIONS, TWO DEADLINES: HOW NOVEMBER RESET THE CRITICAL MINERALS SUPPLY-CHAIN ARITHMETIC FOR WESTERN BUYERS
snippet: InvestorNews' critical minerals analyst Jeff Watkins argues that November 2026 represents a genuine inflection point for Western critical mineral supply chains, driven by four simultaneous events: the November 4 US midterm results (which returned a Congress with strong cross-party support for domestic minerals investment), Australia's October federal election outcome (which retained the critical minerals investment framework), and two hard deadlines — the November 10 expiry of China's rare earth export-control pause and the looming December 31 cutoff for key US domestic mining tax credit provisions. The combined signal, Watkins argues, is that the window for locking in long-term off-take agreements with Western producers at current distressed equity prices may be shorter than investors expect. For the retail investor audience of this site, the practical read is simpler: the same macro correction that has pushed TSXV rare earth and battery metals equities to multi-year lows is coinciding with a policy and procurement environment that is structurally more supportive of domestic supply than any period in the past decade.
